skills.trigger: When evaluating a chest X-ray showing unilateral hemithorax abnormalities (size discrepancy, vascular changes) to distinguish chronic vascular obstruction from acute parenchymal or pleural pathology.
steps: Inspect the affected hemithorax for volume loss (smaller size), oligemia (decreased vascular markings/lucency), and diaphragmatic elevation.

Contrast these findings with acute alternatives: Pneumothorax typically presents with hyperlucency and volume expansion (unless tension); Pleural effusion causes opacity and blunting of costophrenic angles; Consolidation presents as airspace opacity rather than lucency.

Synthesize the triad of hypoplasia (small volume), oligemia, and elevated diaphragm as specific indicators of chronic pulmonary artery obstruction leading to lung underdevelopment, rather than acute processes.

skills.trigger: When analyzing cross-sectional imaging (CT) of the mediastinum/pulmonary hila in patients with suspected large vessel vasculitis or chronic pulmonary hypertension.
steps: Examine the main and branch pulmonary arteries for wall thickening, luminal narrowing, or complete occlusion.
Identify the presence of calcification within the vessel wall or thrombus, which distinguishes chronic inflammatory/arteritic changes from acute bland emboli.

Correlate vessel morphology with downstream lung parenchyma: Chronic arterial obstruction typically results in ipsilateral lung hypoplasia and mosaic attenuation/oligemia, whereas acute embolism usually preserves lung volume initially.
